paras: The threatened lynching of Sam Price took place at Clinton, Hickman County, Kentucky, in January 1888, when a crowd gathered to lynch Price, who was accused of killing Sheriff Henry Winter. Price had been captured in Tennessee and was not on the train the crowd met, so he was not harmed. The episode reached distant papers through short wire dispatches about his capture.

According to a Louisville dispatch of December 31, 1887, Sheriff Winters of Hickman County tried to arrest Sam Price at his home near Clinton, and Price killed him with a double-barreled shotgun. Later accounts said Price asked to enter his mother's house to change clothes and came back to the door with a rifle. A reward was offered for his arrest, given as $2,000 in one dispatch and $1,200 in later ones.

Price was captured in early January 1888 by a man named Brizendine, called a Clinton marshal in a Cairo dispatch and a Fulton detective in a Paducah dispatch. The Cairo report placed the arrest at Dresden, Tennessee, where the local sheriff held Price in jail, while the Paducah report placed it at Gleason, Tennessee. The Ogle brothers were also captured, one charged with assisting in the murder and the other with aiding the escape.

In Clinton, the Paducah dispatch said, excitement was "unabated" and threats of lynching were freely made. When the Illinois Central train passed Clinton on the morning of January 9, a "large and excited crowd" surrounded the depot "for the avowed purpose of lynching Price should he be on board."

Price was kept in the Dresden jail for some time because of the danger of lynching if he were held at Clinton, and was brought to Kentucky a few weeks later. At the end of February 1888, papers reported that a mob of about fifty men had broken into the Clinton jail and hanged Price and William Remus, a Black man accused of killing J. P. Jackson.

The January episode survives in two brief dispatches, both printed on January 14, 1888, in the Western Kansas World and the Macon Beacon. Both ran under "Murderer Captured" headlines, treated Price's guilt as settled, and reported the lynching threats as news without comment. No Kentucky paper's account of the crowd at the depot was found, and no Black-press coverage exists for this period.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Sam Price
bases: A crowd gathered at the Clinton depot to lynch Price if he arrived by train, and threats of lynching were reported at Clinton (A2, A3); this is a threatened, not completed, lynching.

No one was killed in this episode: the crowd at the depot meant to lynch Price, accused of killing Sheriff Winter, but he was not on the train (A2, A3); his later death at the hands of a Clinton mob in February is a separate episode (A5, A6).
Two separate dispatches, from Cairo (A2) and Paducah (A3), report lynching threats at Clinton after Price's capture, though only the Cairo dispatch describes the crowd at the depot.

accounts.label: Cairo dispatch
accounts.gist: Brizendine captured Price at Dresden, Tenn.; when the Illinois Central train passed Clinton a large, excited crowd surrounded the depot intending to lynch Price if he was aboard.

accounts.label: Paducah dispatch
accounts.gist: Price was captured at Gleason, Tenn., by Detective Brizendine of Fulton and was in jail awaiting requisition; excitement at Clinton was unabated and lynching threats were freely made.

framing.detail: Both January items ran under 'Murderer Captured' headlines, call the killing of the sheriff a foul murder, and note the lynching threats as news without comment.

conflicts.note: The later February reports agree with Dresden as the place Price was jailed.
